title: Die and be damned to you if you have any sense of decency or grace about you
html_source: The character “Bello”, vile and indecent himself has just carried out a barrage of indecencies to humiliate Bloom. Joyce then has “him”, with fortified irony, rail against Bloom with “Die and be damned to you if you have any sense of decency or grace about you;” it is Bloom being consigned to the lowest point of Hell – it is he being condemned for immorality by the vilest of wretches. The scene’s counterpoint in The Odyssey is in Book 10 wherein Odysseus begs Circe to let him leave to continue his journey home. She gives him the bad news that, before he can return home he must visit the Land of the Dead – Hell. When Odysseus points out to her that no one has ever visited there and returned, she gives him directions for the trip and tells him of the sacrifices he must make for a successful journey. In fact, Joyce has already placed Bloom at Hell’s depths. Are there to be hints as to how he might find a safe return?
